title: Choosing the Product to Dispense: Massachusetts Generic Interchange, Biological Substitution and the Point-of-Sale Price
topic: Dispensing / Product selection under M.G.L. c. 112, §§ 12D and 12EE, 105 CMR 720.000, 247 CMR 9.05 and 9.19(1)(a), and M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21C
subtopic: How the practitioner's 'no substitution' indication is carried under M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D and 105 CMR 721.020(B), and the invalidity under 105 CMR 721.040(A) of a prescription whose format does not meet that standard; the order of interchange where it is not indicated and the label indication of an interchange under § 12D and 247 CMR 9.05(3)(a) to (d); the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs under 105 CMR 720.000, what its appendix says of products manufactured under the brand's new drug application and what the Department's Circular Letter DCP 22-01-112 says of authorized generics, older descriptions in Department texts that differ from the current statute, the pharmacy's current copy of the list under 247 CMR 9.19(1)(a), and the Department's policy on the effective date of interchangeability and midstream interchange; generic-name prescriptions, the medical-emergency deviation and the Drug Store reach of 247 CMR 9.05; the hospital exemption and the narrow therapeutic index immunosuppressant notice in § 12D; substitution of interchangeable biological products with its notices and records under M.G.L. c. 112, § 12EE; and the lesser-price charge at the point of sale under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21C
learning_objectives: State how a Massachusetts prescription carries the practitioner's 'no substitution' instruction under 105 CMR 721.020(B), why the signature cannot supply it, and why under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription whose format does not meet those conditions is not filled at all.

Apply the order M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D sets where 'no substitution' has not been indicated: an interchangeable abuse deterrent product if one exists, otherwise a less expensive, reasonably available interchangeable product allowed by the current formulary.

Decide whether a product is interchangeable in Massachusetts by working through the two parts of the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs, the Exception List and the exclusions in 105 CMR 720.060, together with what the appendix to 105 CMR 720.000 says of products manufactured under the brand's new drug application and what the Department's Circular Letter DCP 22-01-112 says of authorized generics, and state what 247 CMR 9.19(1)(a) requires a pharmacy to keep on its premises.

State how an interchange is indicated on the label under M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D and 247 CMR 9.05(3)(a) to (d), including what follows the word for a less expensive generic or brand name product and when abbreviations are permitted.

Explain, as Department guidance rather than regulation, when interchange of a newly listed product becomes required and what the Department's policy asks of a pharmacist facing a midstream interchange.
Distinguish a generic-name prescription with no manufacturer specified under 247 CMR 9.05(2) from a brand-name prescription marked 'no substitution'.
Work both limbs of the medical-emergency deviation in 247 CMR 9.05(1), including the record, the purchaser's written acceptance, Board review and the Drug Store reach of 247 CMR 9.05.
Identify which prescriptions the hospital exemption in § 12D removes and which it does not, and when the narrow therapeutic index immunosuppressant notice is owed and to whom.
State when a pharmacist may substitute an interchangeable biological product under M.G.L. c. 112, § 12EE, what bars it, and what notices and records follow, to whom and when.
Work out the charge required at the point of sale under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21C, and name what that section requires of the health benefit plan or carrier and of PBM contracts.

orientation.text: Choosing which product goes into the container is governed in Massachusetts by a small set of provisions that answer different questions, and most errors come from carrying the answer to one question into another. For a prescription generally, and provided the prescription is in the format the Department's standards require, M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D decides the matter: if the practitioner has indicated 'no substitution', the pharmacist dispenses the exact drug product the practitioner indicated, and otherwise the pharmacist dispenses an interchangeable abuse deterrent product if one exists or, if none exists, a less expensive, reasonably available, interchangeable drug product as allowed by the most current formulary. Both directions are subject to the statute's exemption for prescriptions dispensed in a hospital, and the Board's regulation adds a provision for generic-name prescriptions and a medical-emergency deviation, all taken up below. For a biological product prescribed by its trade or brand name, M.G.L. c. 112, § 12EE supplies a permission to substitute an interchangeable biological product, with its own conditions, notices and record. At the register, M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21C fixes what the pharmacy charges. Three neighbouring subjects are named here only where they touch this one: apart from the indication of an interchange, which is taught here, what the label and the dispensing record must show, including the record of which product was dispensed, belongs with the dispensing label and record; the offer to counsel and the counseling itself belong with counseling; and what a prescription must otherwise contain, and when it may be oral or written, belongs with oral prescriptions and prescription format.

The instruction that stops interchange belongs to the practitioner, and the law says how it has to appear. Section 12D requires every prescription issued in the commonwealth by a practitioner to meet the format standards established by the Department of Public Health, and requires those standards to permit the practitioner to instruct the pharmacist to dispense a brand name drug product by indicating 'no substitution'. The Department's standard is 105 CMR 721.020(B), and it attaches three conditions: the indication of 'no substitution' is not the default indication; the prescription indicates that 'Interchange is mandated unless the practitioner indicates "no substitution" in accordance with the law', so the default is stated on the face of the prescription itself; and the indication is a unique element in the Prescription that is not satisfied by any other element, including the signature. The conditions are not confined to one form of prescription: under 105 CMR 721.003 the standards are ones that all prescriptions issued by practitioners or reduced to writing by pharmacists must meet, and 105 CMR 721.020(F) expressly requires a written prescription, where one is permitted, to comply with 721.020(B). The signature matters for a different reason: under § 12D it is only by signing in accordance with the standards that the practitioner validates the prescription. On a validly signed prescription in a conforming format, one that carries the statement and offers the unique, non-default element, a practitioner who has not made that indication has not indicated 'no substitution', because neither the signature nor any other element supplies it, and interchange is mandated. A format that fails the conditions is a different matter. A prescription that makes 'no substitution' the default indication, for example by a pre-printed or pre-selected mark, that does not carry the statement, or that lets the signature or another element serve as the indication does not conform to 105 CMR 721.000, and under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription in a format that does not conform is invalid and shall not be filled: it is filled neither as written nor with an interchangeable product. Neither § 12D nor 105 CMR 721.000 says what the pharmacist does next, such as whether to contact the practitioner; the course that is safe is to dispense nothing on the invalid prescription and to obtain a prescription that conforms. Where the indication is made on a conforming prescription, the pharmacist shall dispense the exact drug product as indicated by the practitioner, and, outside the medical-emergency deviation and the provision for generic-name prescriptions described below, neither the direction to an abuse deterrent product nor the direction to a less expensive interchangeable product applies.

Where 'no substitution' has not been indicated, § 12D gives the pharmacist a duty rather than a discretion, and it is a duty with an order. The first question is whether an interchangeable abuse deterrent drug product exists: a drug with abuse deterrent properties that the drug formulary commission has identified as an appropriate substitute for a drug the commission has determined poses a heightened level of risk to the public due to its potential for abuse and misuse, under M.G.L. c. 17, § 13(b). That subsection provides for the commission's formulary of chemically equivalent substitutions for opiates in schedule II or III, which the Department shall adopt by regulation. If such a product exists, the statute directs the pharmacist to dispense it, and its text attaches no price or availability qualifier to that direction. Only if none exists does the familiar direction apply: a less expensive, reasonably available, interchangeable drug product as allowed by the most current formulary or supplement thereof. An interchangeable drug product is one containing a drug in the same amounts of the same active ingredients in the same dosage form as other products with the same generic or chemical name, and the formulary of interchangeable drug products is the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs established by 105 CMR 720.000. Section 12D also requires the pharmacist to indicate the fact of the interchange on the label, in the form described below. Nothing in § 12D makes a patient's preference for the brand a ground for dispensing it. What the statute gives the drug purchaser or patient is a complaint route: in the event of noncompliance by a pharmacist or a practitioner, the purchaser or patient may inform the director of consumer affairs and business regulation, who shall refer the matter to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and, where appropriate, to the Board of Registration in Medicine.

Interchangeability in Massachusetts is therefore chiefly a question of listing, and 105 CMR 720.050 builds the list in two parts. The first part rests on a federal determination: drug products that FDA considers therapeutically equivalent to other pharmaceutically equivalent products listed with the same generic or chemical name in the most recent edition of Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations, the Orange Book, and its supplements. Under 105 CMR 720.070 those products are deemed interchangeable and added upon publication, but under 105 CMR 720.080 the Department, working with the commission, has authority to review and revise that part as necessary, and those revisions are specified on an Exception List set forth in the appendix at 105 CMR 720.200. The second part is Massachusetts in origin: the Additional List in that appendix, made up of products for which the commission has determined that bioequivalence is not essential or, where it may be essential, that bioequivalence has been established, and which the Department and the commission review at least once a year. The appendix turns this into a lookup. A product whose same drug product, dosage form and strength has been assigned an 'A' rating by FDA in the Orange Book and is not on the Exception List is interchangeable; a product not listed in the Orange Book is looked up by generic name on the Additional List, where the same drug product, dosage form and strength must appear. The lookup is not the whole answer: products manufactured under the same new drug application as the brand name product, and authorized generics, are taken up in the next paragraph. Three kinds of product are excluded by 105 CMR 720.060: a product for which bioequivalence may be essential but has not been established, a product that is the subject matter of patent rights where provision by anyone other than the patent holder would violate the patent, and a product available from only one manufacturer at one price. The list also has to be kept at the pharmacy: under 247 CMR 9.19(1)(a) a pharmacy shall maintain on the pharmacy premises a current copy or electronic version of the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs, including the Orange Book, Additional List and Exception List, a requirement that 247 CMR 9.19(24) does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

Two Department texts reach products that the lookup can miss, and they differ in status. The first is printed in the regulation's own appendix. The Introduction in the appendix at 105 CMR 720.200 states that several generic drug products are manufactured under the same new drug application (NDA) as the brand name drug products, that according to section 1.6 of the Orange Book drug products with the same NDA are therapeutically equivalent, and that Massachusetts regulations allow the interchange of these products. It adds that distributors or repackagers of drug products manufactured under the same NDA as the brand name product are not identified in the Orange Book, and that pharmacists who may not be able to determine if drug products are interchangeable should contact the manufacturers, distributors or repackagers. The second is guidance rather than regulation: the Drug Control Program's Circular Letter DCP 22-01-112, Dispensing Authorized Generics, dated January 14, 2022. It describes an authorized generic, a term it notes is defined in 21 CFR 314.3, as most commonly an approved brand name drug that is marketed without the brand name on its label and is otherwise the exact same drug product as the branded product. Because the authorized generic is identical to the brand name drug, the circular states, it is not specifically listed in the Orange Book but is considered to be therapeutically equivalent to its brand name drug, so a pharmacist may interchange a prescription written for a brand name drug with its authorized generic version provided that the prescriber did not indicate 'no substitution' on the prescription. If the FDA listing of authorized generics does not let the pharmacist determine whether drug products are interchangeable, the circular says the pharmacist should contact the manufacturers, distributors or re-packagers. A product found neither in the Orange Book nor on the Additional List is therefore not ruled out on that ground alone if it is manufactured under the brand's NDA or is the brand's authorized generic, and the interchange remains subject to a 'no substitution' indication, as the circular states and § 12D provides.

One dated caution, as the texts read on 16 September 2026: several Department texts still describe interchange in terms that differ from the current statute. 105 CMR 720.010 speaks of interchange when a prescription written by a practitioner indicates 'interchange'; the Foreword and Introduction printed in the appendix at 105 CMR 720.200 describe a practitioner who wants the brand writing 'no substitution' in his or her own handwriting below the signature line, and the Foreword describes a drug formulary commission of nine members; and part II of the Drug Control Program's policy and its Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs page state the duty as interchange of a less expensive interchangeable product, without the first direction to an interchangeable abuse deterrent product. The current texts are the ones to apply: under § 12D and 105 CMR 721.020(B) interchange is mandated unless the practitioner indicates 'no substitution' as a unique, non-default element that the signature does not satisfy, and neither text requires handwriting; § 12D directs an interchangeable abuse deterrent product first where one exists; and M.G.L. c. 17, § 13(a) now provides for a commission of 16 members.

An interchange also has to show on the label, and two texts say how. Section 12D provides that the pharmacist shall indicate the fact of the interchange on the label in the form 'Interchange (name of exact drug product dispensed)'. The sentence closes the paragraph that directs both the abuse deterrent product and the less expensive product, so it reaches either interchange. 247 CMR 9.05(3), which by its words reaches prescriptions dispensed by a pharmacy with a Drug Store Pharmacy License, spells out what follows the word for a less expensive product. When a less expensive generic drug product has been dispensed, 'interchange' plus the generic name and manufacturer of the product shall appear on the label. When a less expensive brand name drug product has been dispensed, 'interchange' plus either the generic name and manufacturer of the product or the less expensive brand name dispensed shall appear. In addition, the brand name of the prescribed drug product may also appear, the regulation's form placing a brand name after the word 'for' that follows the product actually dispensed. Abbreviations are permissible as long as they are commonly understood, so 'IC' may be used for 'interchange' and manufacturers' names may be abbreviated as shown in the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs. The statute's own form spells the word out, so a label that writes 'Interchange' in full meets both texts. Everything else the container label must carry, and the record of which product was dispensed, is treated with the dispensing label and record.

When a product first appears on the list, the timing is addressed by the Department's Drug Control Program in its Policy on drug interchangeability and midstream interchange, which is guidance rather than regulation. The policy fixes the date of listing by the source of the listing: for a product listed from the Orange Book, the date the edition or supplement is postmarked or posted electronically by the United States Department of Health and Human Services, whichever is first; for a product listed through the Additional List, or under 105 CMR 720.080 through the Exception List, the date that list is published by the Secretary of State in the Massachusetts Register. It defines the effective date of interchangeability as not later than 90 days after the date of listing, states that a pharmacist shall interchange when dispensing a new prescription or a refill presented after that date, and states that there is no requirement to wait the full 90 days to initiate an interchange. The same policy addresses midstream interchange, which it defines as the first time an interchangeable product is dispensed pursuant to a prescription written before the date of listing on which the drug changed from sole source to multi-source. It states that a pharmacist presented with a new prescription or refill that requires midstream interchange shall notify the patient and prescriber of the requirement in those cases in which notification is, in the pharmacist's professional judgment, reasonably indicated for the proper care of the patient; that the notice may be written or oral; that no acknowledgment or response is required; and that what prevents a midstream interchange is a new prescription indicating 'no substitution', which a prescriber may issue at any time. Its statement that a copy of the notification or a notation that it was provided should be maintained in the pharmacy record is phrased with 'should'.

Two provisions of the Board's own regulation, 247 CMR 9.05, bear on the choice of product, and a third says where the regulation applies. Under 247 CMR 9.05(2), on a prescription for a generic name drug product with no manufacturer specified by the prescriber, the pharmacist may select any legally marketed drug product, whether or not it appears in the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs and regardless of whether or not the prescriber has marked 'no substitution', in accordance with the prescriber's intent and the normal exercise of professional judgment. A 'no substitution' mark on such a prescription therefore does not fix a manufacturer; the paragraph is written for the case in which the prescriber has named none. The other provision, the medical-emergency deviation in 247 CMR 9.05(1), is taken up next. As to reach, 247 CMR 9.05(3)(e) provides that 247 CMR 9.05 shall only apply to prescriptions dispensed by a pharmacy with a Drug Store Pharmacy License. The sentence is lettered as the last item of the labeling paragraph, but its words refer to 247 CMR 9.05 itself. The course that is safe on either reading is for a pharmacy that does not hold a Drug Store Pharmacy License not to rely on 247 CMR 9.05(1) or (2) as authority for its product selection.

The medical-emergency deviation in 247 CMR 9.05(1)(a) runs in both directions, and in each it is tied to what is in stock. In a medical emergency a pharmacist may fill a prescription marked 'no substitution' by dispensing a less expensive interchangeable drug product as allowed by the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs if the particular brand is not in stock; and a pharmacist may fill a prescription not marked 'no substitution' by dispensing the brand name product as written if the pharmacist has no less expensive interchangeable drug product in stock to be dispensed. Both limbs are permissions, and 247 CMR 9.05(1)(b) attaches the same three things to either: the pharmacist must record the date, hour and nature of the medical emergency on the back of the prescription or in the computerized pharmacy system; the person purchasing the drug product must indicate acceptance of this deviation from the law in writing; and all such prescriptions shall be clearly identifiable and available for review by the Board. The acceptance is the purchaser's, not the prescriber's, and the regulation does not let the pharmacist's own note stand in for it. 247 CMR 9.05 does not define medical emergency; the record it requires includes the nature of the emergency. One interplay needs care. The statute's direction reaches a less expensive interchangeable product that is reasonably available, the regulation speaks of what is in stock, and neither text says whether a product that is out of stock but readily obtainable is reasonably available. Because the regulation calls dispensing the brand for want of an interchangeable product in stock a deviation from the law permitted in a medical emergency, the course that is safe on either reading is, outside an emergency, to obtain the interchangeable product or a prescription on which the practitioner has indicated 'no substitution', rather than to treat an empty shelf as leave to dispense the brand.

Two further provisions of § 12D decide cases that the general direction does not. The first is the hospital exemption: the provisions of § 12D do not apply to prescriptions dispensed in a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51. It carries two provisos that keep it narrow. All outpatient prescriptions dispensed in a hospital shall be on prescription forms as required by § 12D, and no retail pharmacy, however organized, is exempted. The second is a notice duty for one group of patients. If a patient covered by MassHealth is prescribed a narrow therapeutic index immunosuppressant drug for the treatment of an organ or tissue transplant, the pharmacist shall notify the prescribing physician if a substitution to such a drug is made. The paragraph defines the drug as an immunosuppressant for the treatment of an organ or tissue transplant that has a narrow range in blood concentrations between efficacy and toxicity and requires therapeutic drug concentration or pharmacodynamic monitoring. Each condition narrows it: a patient not covered by MassHealth, a narrow therapeutic index drug that is not a transplant immunosuppressant, or a dispensing in which no substitution is made does not bring it into play. The paragraph states no time and no method for the notice, and it is written as a notice duty rather than as a bar on substituting.

Biological products have their own statute, and it is built differently from § 12D. Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 12EE(b), a pharmacist filling a prescription for a biological product prescribed by its trade or brand name may substitute an interchangeable biological product. That is a permission, not a duty. What may be substituted is fixed by the definition in § 12EE(a), which relies on a federal determination about the particular product: a prescription biological product that FDA has determined to be interchangeable with the prescribed brand name biological product under 42 U.S.C. § 262, or a product approved under 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(2) that FDA has determined to be therapeutically equivalent to the prescribed brand name biological product. The statute gives 'biosimilar' and 'interchangeable' their meanings in section 351 of the Public Health Service Act and keeps them as separate terms, so a product's status as a biosimilar is not the determination the definition asks for. A biological product is itself broadly defined: a virus, therapeutic serum, toxin, antitoxin, vaccine, blood, blood component or derivative, allergenic product, protein other than a chemically synthesized polypeptide, or analogous product, or arsphenamine or a derivative of arsphenamine or any other trivalent organic arsenic compound, applicable to the prevention, treatment or cure of a disease or condition of human beings. The bar in § 12EE(c) has a form of its own. A pharmacist shall not substitute if the prescriber instructs otherwise in writing, and the instruction shall be on a patient-specific basis. A general instruction covering all of a prescriber's patients is not in that form, but because substitution is only a permission, nothing in the statute requires the pharmacist to substitute in the face of it.

Once a biological substitution is made, § 12EE sets out two notices and a record, each with its own addressee and clock. The prescribing practitioner is notified by the dispensing pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee within a reasonable time following the substitution, and § 12EE(d) sets the method in order: a notation in the patient's interoperable electronic health record; or, if the pharmacist does not have the ability to make that notation, facsimile, electronic transmission, or a notation in the patient's record maintained by the pharmacy that is accessible to the practitioner by request. A pharmacist who utilizes an interoperable electronic prescribing technology shall enter the substitution into the patient's electronic health record. The patient, or the patient's authorized representative, is notified following the substitution, and § 12EE(e) requires that notification to be written; it may be conveyed by facsimile, electronic transmission, a notation in the patient's record system shared with the prescriber, or another means consistent with prevailing pharmacy practice in accordance with § 12D. Neither notice is a precondition of the substitution, and the written patient notice is not the offer to counsel, which is a separate duty treated with counseling. Under § 12EE(f) the dispensing pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee, the prescribing provider and the administering practitioner shall retain a record of each substitution for not less than one year from the date of the last entry in the profile record, and the subsection states that it does not limit the Board's professional standards for pharmacists and pharmacies, whose own dispensing records are treated with the dispensing label and record. Under § 12EE(g), in the event of noncompliance by a pharmacist or a practitioner, the purchaser or patient may inform the director of consumer affairs and business regulation, as provided in § 12D.

The last decision is what to charge, and M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21C answers it with a comparison between two defined amounts. At the point of sale a pharmacy shall charge an individual for a prescription drug the lesser of the applicable cost-sharing amount or the pharmacy retail price. Cost-sharing is the amount owed by the individual under the terms of the individual's health benefit plan, a term the section takes from M.G.L. c. 176O, § 1, where it means a policy, contract, certificate or agreement entered into, offered or issued by a carrier to provide, deliver, arrange for, pay for, or reimburse any of the costs of health care services. The pharmacy retail price is the amount the individual would pay for that prescription drug at that pharmacy without using a health benefit plan or any other prescription medication benefit or discount, so a price reached through a benefit or discount, or a price at a different pharmacy, is not the figure compared. Two further subsections address the other parties. A health benefit plan or carrier shall not require an insured to make a cost-sharing payment greater than the amount the pharmacy charged under the comparison, and no contractual obligation between a pharmacy benefit manager and a pharmacist shall prohibit a pharmacist from complying with the section. The actors differ, and questions turn on them: the charging duty is the pharmacy's, the limit on required cost-sharing binds the plan or carrier, and the contract provision protects the pharmacist's compliance.
