worked_examples.scenario: An electronic prescription for a brand-name drug product arrives at a Massachusetts pharmacy. It carries the practitioner's electronic signature, the statement that interchange is mandated unless the practitioner indicates 'no substitution', and a separate 'no substitution' element that is not pre-selected and that the practitioner has left unselected. The prescribed drug is not an opiate. A less expensive interchangeable product allowed by the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs is on the shelf. The patient asks for the brand, and a technician says the signature shows the practitioner wanted exactly what was written.
steps: Look for the practitioner's instruction first. The format conforms, and under 105 CMR 721.020(B) 'no substitution' is a unique element that is not the default and is not satisfied by any other element, including the signature, so the signature validates the prescription under § 12D but does not indicate 'no substitution'. Had the element been pre-selected by default, or the statement been missing, the format would not conform and under 105 CMR 721.040(A) the prescription could not be filled at all.

With no 'no substitution' indication, § 12D directs the pharmacist. The abuse deterrent formulary provided for in M.G.L. c. 17, § 13(b) is a formulary of substitutions for opiates in schedule II or III, so no interchangeable abuse deterrent product is in question for this drug.

The direction is therefore a less expensive, reasonably available, interchangeable drug product as allowed by the most current formulary. The product on the shelf is allowed by the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs, is less expensive and is at hand, so it is the product to dispense, and the fact of the interchange is indicated on the label in the form 'Interchange (name of exact drug product dispensed)'.

Answer the patient. Nothing in § 12D makes the patient's preference a ground for dispensing the brand; what requires the exact product is a prescription on which the practitioner has indicated 'no substitution', and a prescriber may issue one.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacist dispenses the less expensive interchangeable product and indicates the interchange on the label. The error the scenario invites is treating the practitioner's signature, or the patient's request, as the 'no substitution' instruction, when only the practitioner's unique, non-default indication has that effect.

worked_examples.scenario: At a Massachusetts pharmacy holding a Drug Store Pharmacy License, two brand-name prescriptions without 'no substitution' are interchanged. For the first, a less expensive generic product is dispensed and the label shows 'IC' followed by the generic name only. For the second, a less expensive brand name product is dispensed and the label shows 'Interchange' followed by that brand name; a technician wants to add the prescribed brand name after 'for'. A colleague says abbreviations are never allowed on an interchange label.
steps: Start with the statute. Section 12D requires the fact of the interchange to be indicated on the label in the form 'Interchange (name of exact drug product dispensed)', so each label has to show the interchange and the product actually dispensed.

Apply 247 CMR 9.05(3)(a) to the generic. What follows 'interchange' is the generic name and manufacturer of the product, so the first label lacks the manufacturer, whose name may be abbreviated as shown in the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs.

Apply 247 CMR 9.05(3)(b) to the brand. What follows 'interchange' is either the generic name and manufacturer of the product or the less expensive brand name dispensed, so the second label meets the paragraph, and under 247 CMR 9.05(3)(c) the prescribed brand name may also appear after 'for'.

Answer the colleague. 247 CMR 9.05(3)(d) permits commonly understood abbreviations, such as 'IC' for 'interchange'; because the statute's own form spells the word out, writing 'Interchange' in full meets both texts.
worked_examples.resolution: The first label needs the manufacturer added, and the second label is sufficient and may add the prescribed brand name. The error the scenario invites is treating the generic name alone as enough for a generic interchange, or treating 'IC' as forbidden, when the regulation requires the manufacturer and permits commonly understood abbreviations.

worked_examples.scenario: Late on a Saturday night at a Massachusetts pharmacy holding a Drug Store Pharmacy License, a caregiver presents a prescription marked 'no substitution' for a patient in a medical emergency. The particular brand is not in stock; a less expensive interchangeable product allowed by the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs is. The pharmacist plans to dispense it, leave a voicemail for the prescriber, and type 'emergency' into the computerized pharmacy system.
steps: Check the reach and the limb. By the words of 247 CMR 9.05(3)(e), 247 CMR 9.05 applies to prescriptions dispensed by a pharmacy with a Drug Store Pharmacy License, and the limb that fits is a prescription marked 'no substitution' whose particular brand is not in stock, which may be filled with a less expensive interchangeable product allowed by the list.

Complete the pharmacist's record under 247 CMR 9.05(1)(b): the date, hour and nature of the medical emergency, on the back of the prescription or in the computerized pharmacy system. The word 'emergency' alone records neither the hour nor the nature.
Obtain the written acceptance of the deviation from the person purchasing the drug product, here the caregiver. A voicemail to the prescriber is not what the regulation asks for.
Keep the prescription clearly identifiable and available for review by the Board, as 247 CMR 9.05(1)(b) provides for all such prescriptions.
worked_examples.resolution: The dispensing is permitted, but only with the full record, the caregiver's written acceptance and a prescription kept identifiable for Board review. The error the scenario invites is treating a bare note and a message to the prescriber as enough, when the regulation names the date, hour and nature of the emergency and the purchaser's written acceptance.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescription at a Massachusetts Drug Store pharmacy names a drug by its generic name, specifies no manufacturer, and is marked 'no substitution'. The product the pharmacy stocks under that generic name is legally marketed but does not appear in the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs. One pharmacist says the mark forbids changing from the manufacturer dispensed last time; another says only a listed product may be used.
steps: Identify the paragraph. 247 CMR 9.05(2) governs a prescription for a generic name drug product with no manufacturer specified by the prescriber, and it applies regardless of whether or not the prescriber has marked 'no substitution'.
Apply its latitude. The pharmacist may select any legally marketed drug product whether or not it appears in the list, so the stocked product's absence from the list does not rule it out.

Apply its limit. The selection is made in accordance with the prescriber's intent and the normal exercise of professional judgment, so the pharmacist weighs what the prescriber intended in choosing among legally marketed products.
worked_examples.resolution: Any legally marketed product may be selected in accordance with the prescriber's intent and professional judgment. The error the scenario invites is carrying the brand-name meaning of 'no substitution' into a generic-name prescription with no manufacturer specified, or confining the choice to listed products, when 247 CMR 9.05(2) does neither.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacist fills a prescription for a biological product written by its brand name. Two alternatives are in stock: a biosimilar for which FDA has made no interchangeability determination, and a product FDA has determined to be interchangeable with the prescribed brand name product. The prescriber's office once sent a letter preferring no biological substitutions for any of its patients. The pharmacist substitutes the interchangeable product and mentions the change to the patient at pickup.
steps: Test each alternative against § 12EE(a). The biosimilar has no FDA interchangeability determination and is not described as a product approved under 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(2) that FDA has determined therapeutically equivalent, so it is not an interchangeable biological product; the second product is.

Read the letter against § 12EE(c). The bar is an instruction in writing on a patient-specific basis, and a general letter covering all patients is not in that form; substitution is only a permission, so the pharmacist could equally have declined to substitute.

Notify the prescribing practitioner within a reasonable time following the substitution by a notation in the patient's interoperable electronic health record; only if the pharmacist cannot make that notation do facsimile, electronic transmission or a notation in the pharmacy's patient record accessible to the practitioner by request serve instead.
Notify the patient, or the patient's authorized representative, in writing under § 12EE(e); a word at pickup is not a written notification.
Retain a record of the substitution for not less than one year from the date of the last entry in the profile record under § 12EE(f).
worked_examples.resolution: Only the product FDA determined interchangeable may be substituted, and substituting it is lawful here, but the substitution must be followed by the prescriber notice in the order the statute sets, a written patient notice and the retained record. The error the scenario invites is treating biosimilar status as interchangeability, or treating a word at pickup as the written patient notice.

worked_examples.scenario: An insured patient's health benefit plan adjudicates a $25 cost-sharing amount for a prescription drug at a Massachusetts pharmacy. That pharmacy's price for the drug to a customer using no plan, benefit or discount is $19. A pharmacy across town charges $15. The pharmacy's contract with a pharmacy benefit manager says the pharmacist must collect the adjudicated amount.
steps: Identify the two figures § 21C(b) compares. The applicable cost-sharing amount is $25. The pharmacy retail price under § 21C(a) is what the individual would pay at that pharmacy without a health benefit plan or any other prescription medication benefit or discount, which is $19; the $15 price at a different pharmacy is not that figure.
Charge the lesser. At the point of sale the pharmacy charges $19.

Address the contract. Under § 21C(d) no contractual obligation between a pharmacy benefit manager and a pharmacist shall prohibit the pharmacist from complying, so the contract term does not support collecting $25.
Note the plan's side. Under § 21C(c) the health benefit plan or carrier shall not require the insured to make a cost-sharing payment greater than the $19 charged.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacy charges $19. The error the scenario invites is collecting the adjudicated $25 because the PBM contract says so, or treating the $15 price at another pharmacy as the pharmacy retail price, when the comparison is between the applicable cost-sharing amount and that pharmacy's own retail price.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient has taken a brand-name drug for two years on prescriptions that did not indicate 'no substitution'. The drug has become multi-source, and an interchangeable product entered the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs through an Orange Book supplement posted twenty days ago. At the next refill one pharmacist says interchange cannot begin until 90 days have passed; another says it must begin today and the patient must sign an acknowledgment. The prescriber's office telephones to ask that the pharmacy note on the profile that the patient stays on the brand.
steps: Place the dates under the Department's policy, which is guidance. For an Orange Book listing the date of listing is the date the supplement was postmarked or posted electronically, whichever was first; interchange is required for prescriptions and refills presented after the effective date of interchangeability, not later than 90 days after that date, and the policy states there is no requirement to wait the full 90 days.
Recognise the midstream interchange: the refill is dispensed on a prescription written before the date of listing on which the drug changed from sole source to multi-source.

Decide on notice. The policy states that the pharmacist shall notify the patient and prescriber in those cases in which notification is, in the pharmacist's professional judgment, reasonably indicated for the proper care of the patient, that the notice may be written or oral, and that no acknowledgment or response is required.

Answer the prescriber's office. Under the policy what prevents a midstream interchange is a new prescription indicating 'no substitution', and under 105 CMR 721.020(B) that indication is a unique, non-default element of the prescription; a note on the pharmacy profile is neither.
worked_examples.resolution: Under the policy the pharmacist may interchange now and must do so for refills presented after the effective date of interchangeability, gives notice where professional judgment indicates it, and needs no signature. The error the scenario invites is treating the 90 days as a mandatory wait, an acknowledgment as a condition, or a profile note as the prescriber's 'no substitution' instruction.

worked_examples.scenario: Two dispensings happen on the same day. At a retail pharmacy owned and operated by a hospital, a pharmacist believes § 12D does not apply to an outpatient prescription because the pharmacy belongs to the hospital. At a community pharmacy, a patient covered by MassHealth who received a kidney transplant presents prescriptions for a narrow therapeutic index immunosuppressant prescribed for the transplant and for warfarin; the pharmacist substitutes interchangeable products for both and tells only the patient.
steps: Read the hospital exemption with its provisos. Section 12D does not apply to prescriptions dispensed in a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51, but no retail pharmacy, however organized, is exempted, so the hospital's ownership of the retail pharmacy does not take the prescription outside § 12D.

Test the immunosuppressant against the final paragraph of § 12D. The patient is covered by MassHealth, the drug is a narrow therapeutic index immunosuppressant prescribed for the treatment of an organ transplant, and a substitution to such a drug was made, so the pharmacist shall notify the prescribing physician.

Test the warfarin separately. It is an anticoagulant, not an immunosuppressant for the treatment of an organ or tissue transplant, so the notice paragraph does not reach it and its interchange follows the general direction in § 12D.
Note what the notice paragraph does not say: it sets no time and no method for the notice, and it does not by its terms prohibit the substitution.
worked_examples.resolution: The hospital-owned retail pharmacy is bound by § 12D, and the community pharmacist owes the prescribing physician notice of the immunosuppressant substitution but not of the warfarin interchange. The error the scenario invites is reading the hospital exemption as covering a retail pharmacy because of its ownership, or treating a word to the patient as the notice the paragraph directs to the prescribing physician.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 105 CMR 721.020(B), what three conditions attach to the practitioner's 'no substitution' indication?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It is not the default indication; the prescription indicates that 'Interchange is mandated unless the practitioner indicates "no substitution" in accordance with the law'; and the indication is a unique element that no other element, including the signature, satisfies.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the practitioner's signature on a Massachusetts prescription is enough to require the pharmacist to dispense the brand as written.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Under § 12D the signature validates the prescription, and under 105 CMR 721.020(B)(3) the 'no substitution' indication is not satisfied by any other element, including the signature. A form that makes the signature serve as the indication does not conform, and under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription on it is invalid and shall not be filled.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A written prescription for a brand name drug is on a pre-printed form on which 'no substitution' is already marked as the default. What follows under 105 CMR 721.020(B) and 721.040(A)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The form makes 'no substitution' the default indication, so it does not conform to 105 CMR 721.020(B)(1), which 105 CMR 721.020(F) applies to written prescriptions. Under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription in a format that does not conform is invalid and shall not be filled: the pharmacist dispenses neither the brand nor an interchangeable product on it, and the course that is safe is to obtain a prescription that conforms.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where 'no substitution' has not been indicated, what does M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D direct the pharmacist to dispense, and in what order?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An interchangeable abuse deterrent product if one exists; if none exists, a less expensive, reasonably available, interchangeable drug product as allowed by the most current formulary or supplement thereof.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How does M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D define an interchangeable drug product?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A product containing a drug in the same amounts of the same active ingredients in the same dosage form as other products with the same generic or chemical name.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What are the two parts of the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs under 105 CMR 720.050?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Drug products FDA considers therapeutically equivalent to other pharmaceutically equivalent products with the same generic or chemical name in the most recent Orange Book and supplements, and the Additional List of products for which the commission has determined bioequivalence is not essential or, where it may be essential, has been established.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the three categories of drug product excluded from the list by 105 CMR 720.060.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Products for which bioequivalence may be essential but has not been established; products subject to patent rights where provision by other than the patent holder would violate the patent; and products available from only one manufacturer at one price.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: May a pharmacist interchange a brand name drug's authorized generic, which is not specifically listed in the Orange Book, and what is the status of the texts that address it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Yes, provided the prescriber did not indicate 'no substitution'. Circular Letter DCP 22-01-112 (January 14, 2022), which is Drug Control Program guidance, says the authorized generic is considered therapeutically equivalent to its brand name drug and may be interchanged on that condition; the Introduction in the appendix at 105 CMR 720.200, part of the regulation, states that Massachusetts regulations allow interchange of generic products manufactured under the same NDA as the brand name product.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where must a pharmacy keep the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs, and in what form?
retrieval_prompts.answer: On the pharmacy premises, as a current copy or electronic version that includes the Orange Book, Additional List and Exception List, under 247 CMR 9.19(1)(a); 247 CMR 9.19(24) does not apply that requirement to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In what form does M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D require an interchange to be indicated on the label?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 'Interchange (name of exact drug product dispensed)'.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.05(3)(a), what appears on the label with 'interchange' when a less expensive generic drug product is dispensed?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The generic name and manufacturer of the product.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.05(3)(b) and (c), what may appear on the label when a less expensive brand name drug product is dispensed?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 'Interchange' plus either the generic name and manufacturer of the product or the less expensive brand name dispensed; the brand name of the prescribed drug product may also appear.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: May 'IC' be used on an interchange label?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Yes. 247 CMR 9.05(3)(d) permits commonly understood abbreviations, giving 'IC' for 'interchange' as an example, and manufacturers' names may be abbreviated as shown in the list. Because the statute's own form spells the word out, writing 'Interchange' in full meets both texts.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under the Department's policy, when does interchange of a newly listed product become required, and must the pharmacist wait?
retrieval_prompts.answer: For new prescriptions and refills presented after the effective date of interchangeability, which is not later than 90 days after the date of listing; the policy states there is no requirement to wait the full 90 days. The policy is Department guidance.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under the Department's policy, what prevents a midstream interchange?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A new prescription from the prescriber that indicates 'no substitution'; no acknowledgment or response to the pharmacist's notice is required either way.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A generic-name prescription with no manufacturer specified is marked 'no substitution'. What may the pharmacist select under 247 CMR 9.05(2)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Any legally marketed drug product, whether or not it appears in the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs and regardless of the 'no substitution' mark, in accordance with the prescriber's intent and the normal exercise of professional judgment.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In a medical emergency, what may be dispensed on a prescription not marked 'no substitution', and on what stock condition?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The brand name product as written, if the pharmacist has no less expensive interchangeable drug product in stock to be dispensed.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: List everything 247 CMR 9.05(1)(b) attaches to a medical-emergency deviation.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacist records the date, hour and nature of the medical emergency on the back of the prescription or in the computerized pharmacy system; the person purchasing the drug product indicates acceptance of the deviation from the law in writing; and all such prescriptions are clearly identifiable and available for review by the Board.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: To which prescriptions does 247 CMR 9.05 apply by its own words?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Under 247 CMR 9.05(3)(e), prescriptions dispensed by a pharmacy with a Drug Store Pharmacy License.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D reach an outpatient prescription filled at a retail pharmacy owned by a hospital?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Yes. The exemption for prescriptions dispensed in a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51 carries the proviso that no retail pharmacy, however organized, is exempted.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: When must the pharmacist notify the prescribing physician under the final paragraph of M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D?
retrieval_prompts.answer: When a patient covered by MassHealth is prescribed a narrow therapeutic index immunosuppressant drug for the treatment of an organ or tissue transplant and a substitution to such a drug is made.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 12EE(a), what two kinds of product count as an interchangeable biological product?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A prescription biological product FDA has determined to be interchangeable with the prescribed brand name biological product under 42 U.S.C. § 262, or one approved under 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(2) that FDA has determined to be therapeutically equivalent to the prescribed brand name biological product.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What bars a biological substitution under M.G.L. c. 112, § 12EE(c)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An instruction from the prescriber in writing, on a patient-specific basis, not to substitute.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: After a biological substitution, who is notified, when, and in what form?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The prescribing practitioner, within a reasonable time following the substitution, by a notation in the patient's interoperable electronic health record or, if the pharmacist cannot make one, by facsimile, electronic transmission or a pharmacy record notation accessible to the practitioner by request; and the patient or the patient's authorized representative, following the substitution, in writing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: For how long, measured from what, and by whom is the record of a biological substitution kept?
retrieval_prompts.answer: For not less than one year from the date of the last entry in the profile record, by the dispensing pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee, the prescribing provider and the administering practitioner.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does a Massachusetts pharmacy charge at the point of sale under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21C(b)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The lesser of the applicable cost-sharing amount and the pharmacy retail price.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What is the pharmacy retail price under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21C(a)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The amount an individual would pay for the prescription drug at that pharmacy without using a health benefit plan or any other prescription medication benefit or discount.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Can a contract with a pharmacy benefit manager stop a pharmacist from charging the lesser amount?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21C(d) no contractual obligation between a pharmacy benefit manager and a pharmacist shall prohibit the pharmacist from complying with the section.

quick_review.text: Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D a practitioner who indicates 'no substitution' requires the pharmacist to dispense the exact drug product as indicated.

Under 105 CMR 721.020(B) the 'no substitution' indication is not the default, the prescription states that interchange is mandated unless it is indicated, and the indication is a unique element that the signature does not satisfy.

A prescription whose format makes 'no substitution' the default, omits the statement that interchange is mandated, or lets the signature serve as the indication does not conform, and under 105 CMR 721.040(A) it is invalid and shall not be filled.

Where 'no substitution' is not indicated, § 12D directs an interchangeable abuse deterrent product if one exists, and otherwise a less expensive, reasonably available interchangeable product allowed by the most current formulary.

The abuse deterrent substitutions are those identified by the drug formulary commission under M.G.L. c. 17, § 13(b), whose abuse deterrent formulary covers opiates in schedule II or III with a heightened public health risk.
The Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs in 105 CMR 720.000 is the Orange Book therapeutic-equivalence portion, revised through the Exception List, together with the Additional List.

105 CMR 720.060 excludes products whose essential bioequivalence has not been established, patent-protected products where provision by others would violate the patent, and products from only one manufacturer at one price.

Beyond the listing, the Introduction in the appendix at 105 CMR 720.200 states that Massachusetts regulations allow interchange of generic products manufactured under the same NDA as the brand, and Circular Letter DCP 22-01-112, which is guidance, says a brand's authorized generic may be interchanged unless the prescriber indicated 'no substitution'.

Under 247 CMR 9.19(1)(a) a pharmacy keeps on its premises a current copy or electronic version of the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs, including the Orange Book, Additional List and Exception List; institutional sterile compounding pharmacies are excepted by 247 CMR 9.19(24).
Section 12D requires the fact of an interchange to be indicated on the label in the form 'Interchange (name of exact drug product dispensed)'.

Under 247 CMR 9.05(3) a less expensive generic carries 'interchange' with its generic name and manufacturer, a less expensive brand carries 'interchange' with either its generic name and manufacturer or its brand name, the prescribed brand name may also appear, and commonly understood abbreviations such as 'IC' are permitted.

The Department's policy, which is guidance, states that interchange is required for prescriptions and refills presented after the effective date of interchangeability, not later than 90 days after listing, with no requirement to wait.

Under the policy, notice of a midstream interchange turns on the pharmacist's professional judgment, may be written or oral and needs no acknowledgment; a new prescription indicating 'no substitution' prevents the interchange.

247 CMR 9.05(2) lets the pharmacist select any legally marketed product for a generic-name prescription with no manufacturer specified, whether or not the product is listed and whether or not 'no substitution' is marked.

In a medical emergency 247 CMR 9.05(1)(a) permits a less expensive listed interchangeable product when a 'no substitution' brand is not in stock, and the brand as written when no less expensive interchangeable product is in stock.
Either emergency limb requires the recorded date, hour and nature of the emergency, the purchaser's written acceptance, and a prescription clearly identifiable and available for Board review.
By the words of 247 CMR 9.05(3)(e), 247 CMR 9.05 shall only apply to prescriptions dispensed by a pharmacy with a Drug Store Pharmacy License.
Section 12D does not apply to prescriptions dispensed in a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51, but no retail pharmacy, however organized, is exempted.
A substitution to a narrow therapeutic index transplant immunosuppressant for a MassHealth patient requires notice to the prescribing physician.

Under § 12EE a pharmacist may substitute an interchangeable biological product for a biological product prescribed by trade or brand name unless the prescriber instructs otherwise in writing on a patient-specific basis.

After a biological substitution the prescriber is notified within a reasonable time, the patient is notified in writing, and a record is kept for not less than one year from the last entry in the profile record.
At the point of sale a pharmacy charges the lesser of the applicable cost-sharing amount and the pharmacy retail price.
A health benefit plan or carrier may not require a larger cost-sharing payment than the pharmacy charged, and no PBM contract may prohibit a pharmacist from complying.

decision_logic.condition: Before choosing a product, consider where and by whom the prescription is being dispensed.
decision_logic.action: Section 12D does not apply to prescriptions dispensed in a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51, but outpatient prescriptions dispensed in a hospital must be on the required forms and no retail pharmacy, however organized, is exempted. By its words 247 CMR 9.05 applies to prescriptions dispensed by a pharmacy with a Drug Store Pharmacy License.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription's format does not meet 105 CMR 721.020(B): 'no substitution' is the default indication, such as a pre-printed or pre-selected mark; the statement that interchange is mandated unless the practitioner indicates 'no substitution' is missing; or the signature or another element serves as the 'no substitution' indication.
decision_logic.action: Do not fill it. Under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription in a format that does not conform to 105 CMR 721.000 is invalid and shall not be filled, so neither the brand as written nor an interchangeable product is dispensed on it. Neither § 12D nor 105 CMR 721.000 says what the pharmacist does next; the course that is safe is to obtain a prescription that conforms before dispensing.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription for a brand name drug product in a conforming format carries the practitioner's 'no substitution' indication as a unique, non-default element.
decision_logic.action: Dispense the exact drug product as indicated. Neither an interchangeable abuse deterrent product nor a less expensive interchangeable product is put in its place, outside the medical-emergency deviation.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription is in a conforming format, but the practitioner has not made the unique 'no substitution' indication, and the only sign of the practitioner's wishes is the signature or some other element.
decision_logic.action: Neither is the indication 105 CMR 721.020(B) describes, because the indication is not satisfied by any other element, including the signature. Proceed as on a prescription on which 'no substitution' has not been indicated.

decision_logic.condition: 'No substitution' has not been indicated and the drug formulary commission has identified an interchangeable abuse deterrent product for the prescribed drug.
decision_logic.action: Dispense the interchangeable abuse deterrent product; § 12D directs it first and attaches no price or availability qualifier to that direction.

decision_logic.condition: 'No substitution' has not been indicated and no interchangeable abuse deterrent product exists.
decision_logic.action: Dispense a less expensive, reasonably available, interchangeable drug product as allowed by the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs, and indicate the fact of the interchange on the label, as § 12D requires.

decision_logic.condition: The label is being prepared for a product dispensed as an interchange.
decision_logic.action: Indicate the interchange in the form 'Interchange (name of exact drug product dispensed)'. For a less expensive generic product, show its generic name and manufacturer; for a less expensive brand name product, show its generic name and manufacturer or its brand name; the prescribed brand name may also appear after 'for'. Commonly understood abbreviations such as 'IC' are permitted, and writing 'Interchange' in full meets both texts. The rest of the label is governed by the dispensing label rules.

decision_logic.condition: The question is whether a candidate product is interchangeable in Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Look for the same drug product, dosage form and strength rated 'A' in the Orange Book and not on the Exception List; if the product is not in the Orange Book, look for the same drug product, dosage form and strength on the Additional List. Exclude products for which bioequivalence may be essential but has not been established, patent-protected products where provision by others would violate the patent, and products from only one manufacturer at one price. A product found in neither place is not ruled out on that ground alone if it is manufactured under the same NDA as the brand, whose interchange the Introduction in the appendix at 105 CMR 720.200 says Massachusetts regulations allow, or is the brand's authorized generic, which Circular Letter DCP 22-01-112, Department guidance, says a pharmacist may interchange unless the prescriber indicated 'no substitution'. Where a pharmacist cannot determine whether products are interchangeable, both texts point to the manufacturers, distributors or repackagers.

decision_logic.condition: The product was listed as interchangeable only recently.
decision_logic.action: Under the Department's policy, which is guidance, interchange for prescriptions and refills presented after the effective date of interchangeability, not later than 90 days after the date of listing, and interchange sooner if ready. Where the interchange is midstream, notify the patient and prescriber in those cases in which professional judgment indicates it is reasonably needed for the patient's proper care; only a new prescription indicating 'no substitution' prevents it.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription names a drug by generic name with no manufacturer specified.
decision_logic.action: Select any legally marketed drug product, whether or not it is in the list and whether or not 'no substitution' is marked, in accordance with the prescriber's intent and the normal exercise of professional judgment.

decision_logic.condition: A medical emergency exists, the prescription is marked 'no substitution' and the particular brand is not in stock.
decision_logic.action: The pharmacist may dispense a less expensive interchangeable product allowed by the list, then record the date, hour and nature of the emergency, obtain the purchaser's written acceptance, and keep the prescription clearly identifiable and available for Board review.

decision_logic.condition: A medical emergency exists, the prescription is not marked 'no substitution' and no less expensive interchangeable product is in stock.
decision_logic.action: The pharmacist may dispense the brand name product as written, with the same record, written acceptance and availability for Board review.

decision_logic.condition: No medical emergency exists and the less expensive interchangeable product is out of stock but obtainable.
decision_logic.action: Neither text says whether such a product is reasonably available; the course that is safe on either reading is to obtain the interchangeable product, or a prescription on which the practitioner has indicated 'no substitution', rather than dispense the brand.

decision_logic.condition: A patient covered by MassHealth has been prescribed a narrow therapeutic index immunosuppressant drug for an organ or tissue transplant and a substitution to such a drug is made.
decision_logic.action: Notify the prescribing physician; the paragraph sets no time or method and does not by its terms prohibit the substitution.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription is for a biological product prescribed by its trade or brand name and substitution is being considered.
decision_logic.action: Substitute only a product FDA has determined interchangeable with the prescribed brand name product, or one approved under 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(2) that FDA has determined therapeutically equivalent to it; do not substitute where the prescriber has instructed otherwise in writing on a patient-specific basis. Substitution remains a permission.

decision_logic.condition: A biological product has been substituted.
decision_logic.action: Within a reasonable time notify the prescribing practitioner by electronic health record notation or, if that is not possible, by facsimile, electronic transmission or an accessible pharmacy record notation; notify the patient or authorized representative in writing; and retain a record for not less than one year from the date of the last entry in the profile record.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription drug is being sold to an individual who owes cost-sharing under a health benefit plan.
decision_logic.action: Compare the applicable cost-sharing amount with that pharmacy's retail price without any plan, benefit or discount, and charge the lesser; a PBM contract cannot prohibit compliance, and the plan or carrier may not require a larger cost-sharing payment.

ma_vs_federal.text: Massachusetts generic interchange rests partly on a federal determination. The Orange Book portion of the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs consists of products FDA considers therapeutically equivalent, added upon publication; the Exception List and the Additional List are Massachusetts revisions and additions, and a pharmacy keeps the Orange Book as part of its current copy of the list under 247 CMR 9.19(1)(a). The duty to interchange, its order, the label indication and the practitioner's 'no substitution' indication are set by M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D, the Department's standards and the Board's regulations.

For a biological product, M.G.L. c. 112, § 12EE relies on FDA's determination about the particular product: interchangeability with the prescribed brand name product under 42 U.S.C. § 262, or therapeutic equivalence for a product approved under 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(2). The permission to substitute, the prescriber's written patient-specific bar, the two notices and the record are Massachusetts requirements.

Section 12EE(a) gives 'biosimilar' and 'interchangeable' the meanings in section 351 of the Public Health Service Act and builds its definition on FDA's interchangeability determination or, for a product approved under 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(2), FDA's therapeutic-equivalence determination, so biosimilar status is not itself what makes a product an interchangeable biological product under Massachusetts law.

exceptions.text: Hospital: M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D does not apply to prescriptions dispensed in a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51; outpatient prescriptions dispensed in a hospital must still be on the required forms, and no retail pharmacy, however organized, is exempted.

Practitioner's 'no substitution': where it is indicated, the exact drug product is dispensed and neither the abuse deterrent direction nor the less expensive interchange applies, subject to the medical-emergency deviation and, for a generic-name prescription with no manufacturer specified, to 247 CMR 9.05(2).
Medical emergency with the brand out of stock: a prescription marked 'no substitution' may be filled with a less expensive interchangeable product allowed by the list.
Medical emergency with no interchangeable product in stock: a prescription not marked 'no substitution' may be filled with the brand name product as written.
Generic-name prescription with no manufacturer specified: any legally marketed product may be selected, whether or not listed and whether or not 'no substitution' is marked.
Reach of 247 CMR 9.05: by its words it shall only apply to prescriptions dispensed by a pharmacy with a Drug Store Pharmacy License.

Products excluded from the list under 105 CMR 720.060: those whose essential bioequivalence has not been established, patent-protected products where provision by others would violate the patent, and products from one manufacturer at one price.

Products outside the listing: the Introduction in the appendix at 105 CMR 720.200 states that Massachusetts regulations allow interchange of generic products manufactured under the same NDA as the brand, and Circular Letter DCP 22-01-112 (guidance) says an authorized generic, though not specifically listed in the Orange Book, may be interchanged unless the prescriber indicated 'no substitution'.

Reference copy of the list: under 247 CMR 9.19(24) the requirement in 247 CMR 9.19(1)(a) to keep a current copy of the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

Label detail: the forms in 247 CMR 9.05(3)(a) to (d), like the rest of 247 CMR 9.05, by its words apply to prescriptions dispensed by a pharmacy with a Drug Store Pharmacy License; the statutory form in § 12D applies wherever § 12D does.

Newly listed products: under the Department's policy, interchange is required for prescriptions and refills presented after the effective date of interchangeability, not later than 90 days after listing, and may begin sooner.
Biological products: a pharmacist shall not substitute where the prescriber instructs otherwise in writing on a patient-specific basis.

Biological prescriber notice: where the pharmacist cannot make a notation in the patient's interoperable electronic health record, facsimile, electronic transmission or a pharmacy record notation accessible to the practitioner by request is used.

timing_deadlines.event: A drug product is listed in the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Effective date of interchangeability not later than 90 days after the date of listing
timing_deadlines.consequence: Under the Department's policy, which is guidance, interchange is required for new prescriptions and refills presented after that date, and there is no requirement to wait the full 90 days.

timing_deadlines.event: Date of listing for a product listed from the Orange Book
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The date the edition or supplement is postmarked or posted electronically by the United States Department of Health and Human Services, whichever is first
timing_deadlines.consequence: Starts the period in the Department's policy; for the Additional List and the Exception List the date is publication by the Secretary of State in the Massachusetts Register.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least once a year under 105 CMR 720.080; the formularies are revised not less frequently than once a year under M.G.L. c. 17, § 13(b)
timing_deadlines.consequence: Products are added to or deleted from the list on current information about therapeutic efficacy and interchangeability.

timing_deadlines.event: Filling a prescription under the medical-emergency deviation
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The record states the date and hour of the medical emergency, together with its nature
timing_deadlines.consequence: The deviation carries the record, the purchaser's written acceptance and a prescription clearly identifiable and available for Board review.

timing_deadlines.event: Substitution of an interchangeable biological product: notice to the prescribing practitioner
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within a reasonable time following the substitution
timing_deadlines.consequence: The dispensing pharmacist or designee notifies by electronic health record notation or, if the pharmacist cannot make one, by facsimile, electronic transmission or an accessible pharmacy record notation.

timing_deadlines.event: Substitution of an interchangeable biological product: notice to the patient
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Following the substitution; the statute states no number of days
timing_deadlines.consequence: The dispensing pharmacist or designee notifies the patient or the patient's authorized representative in writing.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not less than one year from the date of the last entry in the profile record
timing_deadlines.consequence: Kept by the dispensing pharmacist or designee, the prescribing provider and the administering practitioner.

timing_deadlines.event: Substitution to a narrow therapeutic index transplant immunosuppressant for a MassHealth patient
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The paragraph states no time; the duty arises when the substitution is made
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacist notifies the prescribing physician.

timing_deadlines.event: Sale of a prescription drug to an individual with cost-sharing
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacy charges the lesser of the applicable cost-sharing amount and the pharmacy retail price.

forms_records.text: The prescription carries the statement that 'Interchange is mandated unless the practitioner indicates "no substitution" in accordance with the law', and any 'no substitution' indication is a unique, non-default element that the signature does not satisfy; 105 CMR 721.020(F) applies these conditions to written prescriptions. A prescription in a format that does not meet them is invalid and shall not be filled under 105 CMR 721.040(A).

The label of an interchanged product indicates the interchange in the form 'Interchange (name of exact drug product dispensed)'; under 247 CMR 9.05(3) a less expensive generic shows its generic name and manufacturer, a less expensive brand shows its generic name and manufacturer or its brand name, the prescribed brand name may also appear, and commonly understood abbreviations such as 'IC' are permitted. The rest of the label, and the record of which product was dispensed, are treated with the dispensing label and record.

A pharmacy maintains on its premises a current copy or electronic version of the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs, including the Orange Book, Additional List and Exception List, under 247 CMR 9.19(1)(a); institutional sterile compounding pharmacies are excepted by 247 CMR 9.19(24).
For a medical-emergency deviation, the pharmacist records the date, hour and nature of the emergency on the back of the prescription or in the computerized pharmacy system.
For a medical-emergency deviation, the person purchasing the drug product indicates acceptance of the deviation from the law in writing.
All prescriptions filled under the medical-emergency deviation shall be clearly identifiable and available for review by the Board.
Under the Department's policy, a copy of a midstream interchange notification or a notation that it was provided should be maintained in the pharmacy record; the policy phrases this with 'should'.
The Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs is published in 105 CMR 720.000, with the Additional List and the Exception List in the appendix at 105 CMR 720.200.

After a biological substitution, the prescriber notice is a notation in the patient's interoperable electronic health record or, where the pharmacist cannot make one, a facsimile, an electronic transmission or a notation in the pharmacy's patient record accessible to the practitioner by request; a pharmacist who utilizes interoperable electronic prescribing technology enters the substitution into the patient's electronic health record.

After a biological substitution, the patient notice is written and may be conveyed by facsimile, electronic transmission, a notation in the patient's record system shared with the prescriber, or another means consistent with prevailing pharmacy practice in accordance with § 12D.

A record of each biological substitution is retained for not less than one year from the date of the last entry in the profile record, and § 12EE(f) does not limit the Board's professional standards for pharmacies.

role_duties.role: Prescribing practitioner
role_duties.duty: Issue the prescription in the format the Department's standards require, which under 105 CMR 721.020(B) carries the statement that interchange is mandated unless 'no substitution' is indicated and does not make 'no substitution' the default; to require the exact drug product, indicate 'no substitution' as a unique, non-default element of the prescription. The signature validates the prescription but does not supply the indication.

role_duties.role: Prescribing practitioner facing a midstream interchange
role_duties.duty: Under the Department's policy, prevent the interchange by issuing a new prescription that indicates 'no substitution'; no response to the pharmacist's notice is required.

role_duties.role: Prescriber of a biological product
role_duties.duty: To bar substitution of an interchangeable biological product, instruct otherwise in writing on a patient-specific basis; retain a record of each substitution for not less than one year from the date of the last entry in the profile record.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist filling a brand-name prescription in a conforming format on which 'no substitution' has not been indicated
role_duties.duty: Dispense an interchangeable abuse deterrent product if one exists, otherwise a less expensive, reasonably available interchangeable product allowed by the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs, and indicate the fact of the interchange on the label in the form § 12D sets, with the detail 247 CMR 9.05(3) adds.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist presented with a prescription whose format does not meet 105 CMR 721.020(B)
role_duties.duty: Not fill it, either as written or with an interchangeable product, because 105 CMR 721.040(A) makes it invalid; neither § 12D nor 105 CMR 721.000 says what follows, and the course that is safe is to obtain a prescription that conforms before dispensing.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy
role_duties.duty: Maintain on the pharmacy premises a current copy or electronic version of the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs, including the Orange Book, Additional List and Exception List; 247 CMR 9.19(24) excepts institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist filling a generic-name prescription with no manufacturer specified
role_duties.duty: Select any legally marketed drug product in accordance with the prescriber's intent and the normal exercise of professional judgment, whether or not listed and whether or not 'no substitution' is marked.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist using the medical-emergency deviation
role_duties.duty: Dispense only within the limb that fits the stock position, and record the date, hour and nature of the medical emergency on the back of the prescription or in the computerized pharmacy system.

role_duties.role: Person purchasing the drug product in a medical-emergency deviation
role_duties.duty: Indicate acceptance of the deviation from the law in writing.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist facing a midstream interchange
role_duties.duty: Under the Department's policy, notify the patient and prescriber in those cases in which notification is, in professional judgment, reasonably indicated for the proper care of the patient, in writing or orally.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist substituting for a MassHealth patient's transplant immunosuppressant
role_duties.duty: Notify the prescribing physician when a substitution to a narrow therapeutic index immunosuppressant drug for the treatment of an organ or tissue transplant is made.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist filling a prescription for a biological product by trade or brand name
role_duties.duty: Substitute, if at all, only an interchangeable biological product as § 12EE(a) defines it, and not where the prescriber has instructed otherwise in writing on a patient-specific basis.

role_duties.role: Dispensing pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee after a biological substitution
role_duties.duty: Notify the prescribing practitioner within a reasonable time by the method § 12EE(d) sets, notify the patient or authorized representative in writing, and retain a record of the substitution for not less than one year from the date of the last entry in the profile record.

role_duties.role: Administering practitioner of a substituted biological product
role_duties.duty: Retain a record of each substitution for not less than one year from the date of the last entry in the profile record.

role_duties.role: Drug purchaser or patient
role_duties.duty: May inform the director of consumer affairs and business regulation of noncompliance by a pharmacist or a practitioner with § 12D or § 12EE.

role_duties.role: Director of consumer affairs and business regulation
role_duties.duty: Refer a report of noncompliance with § 12D to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and, where appropriate, to the Board of Registration in Medicine.

role_duties.role: Board of Registration in Pharmacy
role_duties.duty: Receives referrals of noncompliance with § 12D, and has medical-emergency deviation prescriptions available for its review.

role_duties.role: Drug formulary commission and Department of Public Health
role_duties.duty: The commission prepares the formularies and the Department adopts them by regulation; the Department, working with the commission, reviews the Additional List at least once a year and specifies revisions to the Orange Book portion on the Exception List.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy at the point of sale
role_duties.duty: Charge the individual the lesser of the applicable cost-sharing amount and the pharmacy retail price.

role_duties.role: Health benefit plan or carrier
role_duties.duty: Not require an insured to make a cost-sharing payment for a prescription drug greater than the amount charged under § 21C(b).

role_duties.role: Pharmacist under a contract with a pharmacy benefit manager
role_duties.duty: Comply with § 21C; no contractual obligation between the pharmacy benefit manager and the pharmacist shall prohibit that compliance.

common_traps.text: Treating the practitioner's signature as 'no substitution', or interchanging on a prescription whose 'no substitution' is a pre-selected default. On a conforming prescription the indication is a unique, non-default element that the signature does not satisfy; a prescription in a format that makes 'no substitution' the default, omits the statement that interchange is mandated or lets the signature serve as the indication is invalid under 105 CMR 721.040(A) and is not filled at all.
Starting with price. Where an interchangeable abuse deterrent product exists, § 12D directs it first, and the text attaches no price or availability qualifier to it.
Dispensing the brand because the patient prefers it. Section 12D makes the practitioner's 'no substitution' indication, not the patient's preference, the ground for dispensing the exact product.

Treating any cheaper generic as interchangeable. The product must be allowed by the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs or fall within the Department's statements on products manufactured under the brand's NDA and authorized generics; products whose essential bioequivalence is unestablished, patent-protected products and single-source products at one price are excluded from the list.

Ruling out a brand's authorized generic because it is not specifically listed in the Orange Book or on the Additional List. Circular Letter DCP 22-01-112, which is Department guidance, says it is considered therapeutically equivalent to its brand name drug and may be interchanged unless the prescriber indicated 'no substitution'.
Showing a generic interchange on the label with the generic name alone. 247 CMR 9.05(3)(a) requires the generic name and manufacturer of the product with 'interchange'.

Treating the prescribed brand name as a required part of the interchange label, or treating 'IC' as forbidden. Under 247 CMR 9.05(3)(c) the prescribed brand name may also appear, and 9.05(3)(d) permits commonly understood abbreviations.
Treating the Orange Book alone as the Massachusetts list kept at the pharmacy. The current copy under 247 CMR 9.19(1)(a) includes the Orange Book, the Additional List and the Exception List.
Carrying the brand-name meaning of 'no substitution' into a generic-name prescription with no manufacturer specified, to which 247 CMR 9.05(2) applies regardless of the mark.
Running the medical-emergency deviation in one direction only. It also permits the brand as written when no less expensive interchangeable product is in stock.
Taking the emergency acceptance from the prescriber, or treating the pharmacist's note as enough. The regulation names the person purchasing the drug product and requires the acceptance in writing.
Stopping at the emergency record and the written acceptance. The deviation prescriptions shall also be clearly identifiable and available for review by the Board.

Treating an empty shelf as ending the interchange direction outside an emergency. Section 12D speaks of a reasonably available product, and 247 CMR 9.05(1) treats dispensing the brand for want of stock as a deviation permitted in a medical emergency, so the safe course is to obtain the interchangeable product or a 'no substitution' prescription.
Reading the hospital exemption as covering a retail pharmacy because of its connection to a hospital. No retail pharmacy, however organized, is exempted.

Extending the § 12D immunosuppressant notice to every narrow therapeutic index drug or every patient, or sending it to the patient. It is confined to MassHealth patients and transplant immunosuppressants, and it goes to the prescribing physician.
Treating the Department's 90 days as a waiting period, or its 'should' about keeping a copy of a midstream notice as a regulatory mandate.

Treating a biosimilar as interchangeable. Section 12EE requires FDA's interchangeability determination or, for a product approved under 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(2), FDA's therapeutic-equivalence determination.
Reading 'may substitute' in § 12EE(b) as 'must substitute'.
Giving an oral notice of a biological substitution to the patient, or treating the prescriber notice as a precondition. The patient notice is written, and both notices follow the substitution.
Measuring the biological substitution record from the dispensing date rather than from the date of the last entry in the profile record.
Collecting an adjudicated cost-sharing amount above the pharmacy retail price because a PBM contract calls for it.
Using a price reached through a benefit or discount, or another pharmacy's price, as the pharmacy retail price.

drug_examples.teaching_point: Oxycodone, a schedule II opioid analgesic, is the kind of drug to which the formulary of abuse deterrent substitutions for schedule II and III opiates in M.G.L. c. 17, § 13(b) is addressed. On a prescription without 'no substitution', § 12D asks first whether the drug formulary commission has identified an interchangeable abuse deterrent product for the prescribed drug; only if none exists does the pharmacist turn to a less expensive, reasonably available interchangeable product.

Warfarin is an anticoagulant, not an immunosuppressant for the treatment of an organ or tissue transplant, so the § 12D notice paragraph does not reach its substitution even for a MassHealth patient; its interchange follows the general direction, and a practitioner who wants the exact product indicates 'no substitution'.
